claims.claim: white perch prefer level bottoms of silt, mud, sand or clay — in Sebasticook Lake, Maine they used soft muck, gravel and rock less (AuClair 1956, via Stanley & Danie 1983)
claims.note: Thesis not readable. Stanley & Danie (PDF p. 14 of the fetched profile) write: 'Soft muck, decomposing organic substrate, or gravel and rocks were found by AuClair (1956) to be less utilized by white perch.' The paper's wording matches the secondary account (it drops 'decomposing organic substrate'); Stanley & Danie do not name Sebasticook Lake in that sentence (the thesis title does).

claims.claim: white perch winter at 12–18 m in deep lakes (AuClair 1956; Sheri & Power 1969; both via Stanley & Danie 1983)
claims.note: Thesis not readable. Stanley & Danie (PDF p. 14): 'White perch overwinter at depths to 40 m (131 ft), but usually at 12.2 to 18.3 m or 40 to 60 ft (AuClair 1956; Sheri and Power 1969).' Which part (if any) is from the Sebasticook thesis and which from Sheri & Power's Ontario work cannot be told from the secondary account.

claims.paper: Table 3.6-1 (white perch, spawning: 'an unpublished thesis via Stanley & Danie 1983 gives 18–21 °C "for several days"')
claims.claim: the temperature must hold at 18–21 °C for several days before white perch spawn in Maine lakes
claims.note: THE LEAD. The thesis itself could not be read, so what AuClair wrote in 1956 is still unknown. The only account is Stanley & Danie 1983 (PDF p. 13 of the fetched profile): 'The temperature must remain at 18° to 21°C (64° to 70°F) in Maine lakes for several days prior to spawning (AuClair 1956).' AuClair's popular account two years later (AuClair 1958, read for that entry) says Maine white perch spawn 'when the temperature of the water is up to 60° F' (15.6 °C), usually in June. The two cannot be reconciled without the thesis. The table should name it (AuClair 1956, M.S. thesis, via Stanley & Danie 1983) rather than 'an unpublished thesis'.
